While we held short of C1, we received additional clearance to continue taxi via Z; we did not realize that Zulu taxiway begins in the intersection between C, C1. In addition there are no signs to provide situational awareness that we were leaving Taxiway Charlie and joining a new Taxiway Zulu, looking back the only indication we had was our heading indicators. As a result, we made a left turn on Charlie 1 and crossed the departure end of Runway 28R and joined Sierra 3. Recommendations, when taxing Northwest bound on Charlie, to join Zulu, the heading reference should remain 281 degrees until passing Charlie 1, after this point, the headings should begin to gradually decrease slowly to about 270 degrees, followed by a heading to about 190 degrees until abeam the departure end of the runway. A sharp turn to about a heading of 170 degrees from Charlie to Charlie 1 will head the aircraft to cross Runway 28R. Taxiway Zulu becomes Taxiway Bravo at B1, when heading Southeast on Bravo, Taxiway Juliet and Foxtrot can be easily confused, and both taxiways will take you across Runway 01L, once again a heading reference must be made. This area needs additional signs and indications.

synopsis: While attempting to fly a G1000 equipped C172 the pilot became confused by both the aircraft equipment and airport layout reluting in a wrong ruway takeoff.

The purpose of the flight was that I would be familiar with the G1000, and to meet a friend about 1 hour of flying from my departure airport. Another thing that I wanted to solo that day was I had never rented the airplane from the school to fly just by myself (I always flew with an instructor for my IFR training). There were a lot of details from my training lessons that I tried to recall besides trying to use the complex avionics. By trying so many new things, so that I could develop the "right" habits, I became overwhelmed with the information. After doing the run up at the ramp I tried to input the destination airport ID to the GPS, and to my surprise I could not remember which knobs to turn to input the airport ID. After trying to enter the airport ID in the GPS for about 10 minutes I decided that I needed to return to the school to review the manual how to use the GPS, so I taxied back to the parking area at the school. I lost my confidence in my ability of using the G1000. An instructor told me to use the FMS knobs for imputing the airport ID, and then I remembered the functions of the FMS knobs. I went through the starting procedures of the airplane again, trying to taxi it the right way as my instructor taught me. There were a lot of things that I had to recall besides trying to operate the airplane by following the PFD and the MFD's indicators. I did not have the confidence like my flying of hundreds of hours in steam gauge airplanes. When the Ground Control cleared me to taxi on the Taxiway Echo, I believe, to the active Runway 21R. I was confused because the Taxiway Echo was nowhere near to where I was at. When I asked for a progressive taxi, Ground Control changed the taxi way to Charlie which was nearby my airplane. I carefully taxied to the active runway but my mind was preoccupied with the multiple data from the PFD and the MFD. At Charlie I repeated the Tower's clearance to "Cleared for take off on Runway 21R, turn right", and I glanced on the runway diagram on the MFD; the letter 23R located at the end of the runway on my left. In confusion, I turned left to line up the airplane thinking that I was lining up with the runway "23R", and took quickly took off because there was another airplane right behind me. I just took off on Runway 5R instead of the Runway 23R on the other direction. During my climbing I was still trying to sort out the data from the PFD (heading, flight path to destination, attitude, etc.) and the MFD (engine RPM, oil, pressure, etc.) then I heard the Tower asking me if I was with a flight instructor. I was surprised to hear that. That question was very unusual during a take off. Why did they ask me that? I replied that "No." When I questioned the Tower if I was cleared to turn right for my west bound, the Tower quickly told me to turn left (because I took off at the opposite runway). synopsis: The pilot of a PA28 at an enroute airport assumes the Tower is closed when unable to reach them on Tower/CTAF. After taxiing out and crossing a runway, a fuel truck stops by and advises that Tower is trying to contact them. Pilot discovers volume knob turned all the way down.
narrative: This incident occurred while I, operating as solo PIC of a Piper Archer 180, was returning home from a family trip with my wife and infant son. After a stopover to refuel and feed our baby in ZZZ at the FBO, the sun had set and we were preparing to depart for the last leg of our journey home. On the ramp, I powered up and used a flashlight to check around the panel due to the low light level in the cockpit. The avionics in the cockpit must individually be powered on and off due to the setup and procedure in that aircraft. Once my checks and preparations were complete, I checked the weather on Radio 2. I called Ground on Radio 1. No answer. I believe I made two attempts to call Ground. I double checked my frequencies. It was dark. It seemed later than it probably was and the airport was completely quite with no traffic. Remembering from the preflight that the Tower is not open 24 hours, I assumed that the Tower must have closed. I contacted Tower on Radio 1 to see if they were open. No response. With the assumption that the Tower was closed and having double checked the frequencies and checked the weather, I proceeded to commence taxi operations using the CTAF (also Tower frequency) to declare my location and intentions using appropriate practices for taxing at an uncontrolled field. I announced my intentions to taxi from the ramp via taxiway Charlie to Runway 31. Approaching the crossing Runway 23, I stopped, turned on [all] lights, including landing lights and strobes, checked for traffic, and announced my crossing on the CTAF. While continuing to taxi down Charlie, I noticed the runway lights flicker. I thought I had accidentally turned them on or off, and I then attempted to bring the lights back up by clicking on the CTAF. I could not see if the lights had indeed come up, so I decided I would check while holding short which, I deduced, would give me a better vantage point of the lights. Holding short of Runway 31, I began my runup procedures and noticed a FBO truck pull up next to me. I idled the aircraft and was informed verbally by the FBO employee that the Controller was trying to reach me. Checking my radios, I realized that the volume receive knob on Radio 1 was not in the correct position for me to hear the Controller. I made contact with the Ground Controller, who asked some questions, notified me that she had attempted to get my attention by flickering the lights, and vented her frustration. Having discussed the situation with the Controller, I then departed with no further incident. The number one factor was a simple human error resulting from having to individually toggle switches for the avionics and radios at each startup. Likewise, the knobs are not lit, and the problem occurred at night. I was using a flashlight, but did not notice the position of the small white line location on the radio volume knob. I was also unable to receive any light gun signals from the Tower, since the Tower was directly behind my taxi direction. To my knowledge no light gun signal was given, due to this reason. It was also only a few minutes before the Tower actually did close, which did not help with my perceptions. Minor fatigue may have also been a factor. Hindsight is 20/20 and having replayed the situation in my head many times in the day after the flight, the seriousness of the incident has sunk in all the more. The day after the incident I tried to make contact via phone with the Controller to express my apologies. I was unsuccessful, but left a message. In the future I will definitely check squelch as part of my startup procedure to ensure that I am getting an appropriate signal. It would also be helpful to include a master avionics toggle switch in that aircraft that would prevent having to turn the volume/power switch (Garmin 430) to the off position, but it would instead allow the volume to remain in a default location to reduce the likelihood of low volume settings.

synopsis: A SR20 pilot had a runway incursion at PHL airport.
narrative:
At PHL airport I crossed over one of the active runways, Runway 27R. I had rented a Cirrus SR20 to fly to a meeting in Philadelphia that day and the 2 Garmin 430s were very poor - I got complaints along the way to Philadelphia from the controllers. I was taxiing from the FBO, crossing over an active runway and holding short at Runway 35. The Ground Controller says he said hold short at Runway 35 INTERSECTION, presumably for an intersection takeoff. I was having difficulty hearing him, so he may have said that. I don't think I repeated that though, as I could not hear him very well through the static. The second runway I crossed on my way to hold short at Runway 35 was Runway 27. I called the number the Ground Controller gave me when I landed. I spoke with one of the controllers at Philadelphia airport and immediately apologized. I was embarrassed, made more obvious by sitting in the penalty box for a while at the airport. The man explained what their version of the communication was, and I told him mine. I asked him to review the tapes and he said they did and that they were talking to the Controller right then. I took this to mean that I was right; I hadn't repeated what the Controller had said, although he followed up with the fact that there is a rule that a Controller cannot clear you to pass over 2 runways. I told him that I was unaware of that rule, and did not believe I had read it in either my private or instrument classes. I said I would go back and review that section in my classes, but he said it was a recent rule within the last 4-5 months.

That was my first flight into a larger airport. This is not meant as an excuse, just an explanation of why something like this might have occurred. I can assure you that I take Aviation Safety seriously - that is why I immediately got my Instrument rating after my Private and am currently finishing up my multi engine Instrument rating - a considerable investment, but I hope to one day take my family (wife and 3 kids with me and I want to be SAFE. I already have a different career, but when I am in the air (or on the ground in a plane for that matter) I have every intention of being the safest and best pilot I can be. What am I doing about it? I will spend a lot more time reviewing unfamiliar airport layouts. I upgraded my Foreflight subscription to alert me (both audibly and visually) to approaching runways as well geo referencing me on airport. I now carry a hand held back up radio in my flight bag. I will continue to read all the magazines I can get my hands on (I am a member of AOPA and read all their magazines). I work my way through the "KING" courses - about 2 a month. When I finish my multi engine course (hopefully this week) I will be hiring a local instructor once a week to practice approaches over and over again with me until I am more comfortable. In short, I spend most of my free time trying to become a safer, better pilot. If you have any advice for me, or anything I might be missing, I would love to take action on it.

synopsis: P46T pilot enters what he believed to be Taxiway A at VGT but turns out to be Runway 07.  Pilot had an earlier issue with his radios which added to his distraction.
narrative: I was in the approximate location of the Runway 7 run-up area and had just completed a run-up. I notified ground control that I was proceeding to what I perceived to be the hold short line for runway 12R. I believe that I was on taxiway A but Ground Control may have been concerned that I was in fact proceeding on runway 7. In any event, I was proceeding eastward on either taxiway A or runway 7 (which was not active at the time) and I know now that I was disoriented and should have not been proceeding on either of them.   Ground Control ordered me to halt at once and proceed no farther and I immediately complied.  Ground referred me to the tower and the tower directed me to make my first left turn onto runway 12R and back taxi to departure end of 12R.  The background of this incident is as follows: I landed at North Las Vegas airport (VGT) in mid-afternoon to re-fuel with the intention to thereafter proceed to my destination of Oakland, California (OAK).  I had never been at VGT and so requested progressive taxi instructions to the FBO upon landing.  The FBO parked me a little southeast of taxiway H.  After the plane had been fueled, I did a pre-flight and started the engine at approximately XA38 local time.  I listened to ATIS and called Clearance Delivery to pick up my IFR clearance.  As I was entering my clearance into my Garmin, my radios emitted a loud static feedback noise.  I had never heard the noise before and tried to correct it by re-tuning the radios, switching radio 1 with radio 2, checking the mic buttons to make sure nothing was stuck, rechecking all switches, etc.  The noise did not go away and remained loud in my headset even with the radio volume turned down.  I finished entering the relatively complicated  clearance instructions, studied the SID and the route and then called Ground Control. synopsis: A pilot took off on Runway 33 when cleared to takeoff on Runway 6R.
narrative: I had recently moved my plane to a hangar at RYN and was taking my first flight from RYN to familiarize myself with the RYN environment and to do some practice instrument approaches at CGZ. RYN Ground said to taxi to 6R via B2 and B and hold short of 33. I complied and called back when I reached 33, reported holding short of 33 and said I would do my run-up. Upon completion of my run-up, I contacted Tower and reported that I was ready for takeoff. I was told that I was clear for 6R. I rolled onto the runway and took-off. As I left the ground and checked my bearing I was shocked to see that I was on a 330 heading. There were no conflicts and when I came back that evening I apologized for my mistake. I still felt terrible for making such an error. I went onto the [internet] and downloaded another runway diagram and studied all the information that was available and have notice that the particular spot that confused me is also the one Hot Spot that is shown for the RYN runway diagram. When one taxis to 33 via B, you have to make a 180 degree turn using 33 to get onto 6R. This can be a real "gotcha" for a pilot that is unfamiliar with the runway configuration, I think. It seems to me that there is one way to make it safer and that would be to taxi to 33 via B to D to 6R and there would still be plenty of takeoff distance. But, there is no run-up area on D. However, there is on B, just before D. Finally, I should have told the controllers at the beginning that I was new to the airport and gotten progressive guidance. I have thought long and hard about this experience since I take a lot of pride in my flying. I hope that I have not overdone my write-up.

synopsis: Corporate jet Captain reported landing on the wrong parallel runway on a night visual approach.
narrative:
Enroute and initial approach went without a hitch. There were thunderstorms along planned STAR so we were moved onto one with a more favorable orientation to weather. We were expecting Runway 22 and that changed to an ILS/visual 12R halfway into to STAR but that was not a big issue. I started feeling a little pushed when we asked for lower but ATC had to hold us up for traffic out of IAH, as a result we ended up at 6,000 FT with less than 10 miles to the airport. ATC turned us onto a downwind heading and finally gave us a descent to 2,000 FT so I expedited to get down since we were trying to get a visual on the airport. We were maneuvering north of the airport when I finally got it in sight. ATC asked if we had it insight (it was at my 9:30 position under a little cloud so difficult for pilot not flying to see) and I said "yes" to [the co-pilot] who advised ATC and we were cleared for a visual approach. I was looking outside maneuvering around the last few clouds keeping the airport insight and simply picked up on 12L, which was the one closest to us. Sad thing is we even had the ILS for 12R tuned up but I was focused on the outside and simply missed this since we were turned well inside the FAF. Approach was stable and Tower never said a word. It was not until the runway markings came insight (it was still dark) that the [co-pilot] made the comment "I think we just landed on the wrong runway". My response was "I thought they cleared us for the visual 12L" and he said "Yes, the visual, but that was for 12R." 

As we taxied to the FBO the Tower never said a word to us and we decided it was best not to discuss this on the radio. After we got shutdown I phoned the Tower to discuss the issue. They confirmed the error, thanked me for the call, then said that it was not a problem due to the early hour and lack of traffic so they'd decided not to say anything to us. They also said they were not going to take any further action and thanked me again for the call.
Classic situation; a little tired from an early get-up combined with subtle pressure of being a little late on a recovery trip, then throw in a little weather, a few ATC changes, a late descent, a visual approach with some clouds and the stage is set for some confusion. 
Lessons learned; slow down, take a little extra time, and always confirm both pilots agree on the runway cleared to land on. Maybe we should consider having this added as the last item on the Before Landing Checklist.

synopsis: A C-172 pilot rushed to become airborne after receiving Runway 14L takeoff clearance and mistakenly turned right onto 32R. Subsequently, Tower commanded an abort because of traffic on a crossing runway.
narrative:
This pilot deviation on the runway was caused by me as the pilot not fully briefing myself before takeoff. I was in a hurry to get my flight done in order to get to my next class in time and decided to not properly brief myself with a takeoff briefing before entering the active runway. Upon entering the runway, instead of turning left onto Runway 14L, I turned right onto Runway 32R. I wasn't paying attention to the fact if I was on the correct runway and proceeded to takeoff at which point the Tower called up and said "Abort takeoff clearance". They then gave me instructions to "When able do a 180 on the runway and proceed with takeoff". That is the point I realized I had started to takeoff down the opposite runway but still followed their instructions and made a 180 on the runway and proceeded with takeoff. The rest of the flight went fine and upon landing I was instructed to contract Tower for possible pilot deviation. What I was not aware of during this occurrence was the fact that there was another airplane also taking off on a crossing runway. While they were already on the climb out, I had apparently crossed into the intersection while doing my 180 degree turn and that's where most of the fault was at. The fact that I had crossed the hold short lines into another active runway while another plane was on the climb out is what was dangerous. 

My decision to rush the flight and skip important steps that would have otherwise prevented this was a poor decision on my part. The obvious mistake for me was to skip the takeoff briefing to reassure myself of which runway I was taking off on. This being the case I have now learned the importance of being a meticulous pilot not only in the air but also on the ground. Whenever I am tempted to rush a flight or skip some things that would expedite my flight I can look back and think of this situation to rectify that feeling. I can also use this as a teaching point for later down the road of when I obtain my CFI as a great example of how hazardous these attitudes can be. Thankfully nobody was hurt but something bad could have happened and this serves as a great example of that.

synopsis: A PC12 pilot was told by DWH Ground Controller they had crossed the hold short line for Runway 17. The pilot does not believe they had taxied past the line and suggests a tree blocked the Ground Controllers view.
narrative: After engine start and IFR clearance obtained [I was] located on the west side of David Wayne Hooks Airport, we were instructed to taxi to Runway 17R via taxiway Echo. A Cirrus SR22 came out of the FBO in a hurry in which I informed Ground Control we would give way to the Cirrus. The Cirrus elected to depart Runway 17R at Intersection Echo well before we made it to the hold short line. As I came to a stop at the hold short line, I contacted Ground and asked if we were cleared to cross Runway 17R. A response from Ground Control stated that we were past the hold short line and to make a 180 degree turn to get behind the hold short line. I replied that "we were up to the short line". To satisfy the Controller, I made the 180 degree turn and taxied further back. I contacted Ground Control again to notify him that we needed full length and was instructed to "contact Tower". [I] contacted Tower "requesting full length for Runway 17R". Tower cleared me to back taxi, and then cleared me for take-off with a right turn to 270 degrees. In this situation, I believe that the Ground Controller made some assumptions that we would just depart at Intersection Echo and Runway 17R. This intersection is almost half of the 7,009 FT of usable runway. Whether I'm flying a Cessna 150 or a Pilatus PC12, I use every inch of available runway for take-off operations. This is standard operating procedures in all the flying I do (professional or personal). Safety is paramount in this business of flight operations. I also believe that the Tower is hidden with tree obstructions on the west side of the field and determining an exact position of an airplane could be somewhat challenging. At no time were we in danger of a runway collision (no landing traffic on Runway 17R and departing Cirrus was on their climb out). Initially, we were up to and holding short of Runway 17R and Echo. Additionally, I believe that controllers should maintain a professional attitude over the frequencies.

synopsis: Small aircraft pilot took off from HYI on Taxiway J thinking it was Runway 13.
narrative: Cleared to taxi to Runway 13 at San Marcos. We had a current airfield diagram, but had difficulty following the taxi instructions due to airfield construction and several barricaded runways/taxiways. Eventually held short of what we thought was Runway 13 for runup. Cleared for takeoff by Tower, we turned from Taxiway C onto what we thought was Runway 13, but in actuality was Taxiway J. We should have been alerted by the markings on Taxiway J, and by a pre-takeoff compass check that we were on the incorrect runway, but did not realize our error until we passed the arrival end of Runway 13 on takeoff roll. We then proceeded on takeoff leg and advised Tower of our error. No traffic conflicts occurred. Lessons learned: Have both pilots review and confirm taxi routes to the active runway after receiving taxi instructions from ground control. Do not rely on previous experience at a particular airport to influence perceptions of ground operations, particularly when a large part of the airfield is under construction (and it is the first visit to the field in a year). Request progressive taxi instructions when in doubt. Confirm that compass and runway headings agree prior to pushing the power up, even in day VFR conditions.

synopsis: AC90 pilot is given taxi instructions from FBO to Runway 31 at PIA. Immediately after pilot begins to taxi Ground Control changes his departure Runway to 13 and his taxi clearance. narrative: I received my initial taxi clearance to taxi to runway 31 from the FBO ramp via taxiway papa, alpha and echo, I wrote the clearance down. synopsis: A helicopter crew failed to hold short of Runway 22R at LFT.
narrative: While conducting run-up and pre taxi checks, crew contacted Lafayette Ground Control requesting taxi instructions for active Runway 22L for IFR departure. Upon hearing this, we as a crew conferred and agreed that, no "Hold Short" instructions were given in the initial or subsequent taxi clearances and that we had acted in a safe and prudent manner, not endangering any other traffic or personnel on the airfield. The remainder of the flight was conducted without incident and upon landing; we as the crew contacted Lafayette Tower control as instructed, giving pilot in command name and certificate number. As corrective action, we researched taxi clearances as per the FAR AIM and conferred with an FAA Examiner to clarify Hold Short instructions to an inactive runway. synopsis: A PA28 pilot crossed the hold short bars at SMO's Runway 21 after mistakenly taking another aircraft's clearance.
narrative: Holding short of Runway 21 waiting for an IFR release, we were experiencing periodic static in our active radio. While waiting, a couple other aircraft took off VFR, but at the time of the runway incursion we were alone at the hold short line, as I recall. I was antsy to takeoff, as the IFR departure delays out of SMO can be substantial. Eventually, we heard "...cleared for immediate takeoff" with the tail number at the beginning lost in a blast of static. I assumed it was for us, since I thought we were the only one at the hold short line, and told my student to start moving to takeoff because there was an aircraft on final. After crossing the hold short bars, Tower told us the takeoff clearance was not for us and I brought the plane to an immediate stop, prior to the runway edge marking. I requested immediate instructions from the Tower, who told us to cross the runway and hold on the other side. I taxied very quickly and held as instructed at the hold bars on the other side of Runway 21. I was clear of the runway well before the traffic on final crossed the fence. My impatience to depart, coupled with the radio problem, led me to make a hasty decision to accept an unclear takeoff clearance, and I should have verified with Tower, as I always do. Even if it meant losing my "immediate" clearance, it isn't worth a runway incursion.

synopsis: An attempt by Ground Control to expedite operations resulted in the reporter's aircraft crossing the hold short line and stopping while another continued its takeoff despite the encroachment and a third on short final executed a go-around.
narrative:
Our taxi clearance was, "Taxi to Runway 30L, via Y, C, M, and hold short of 4 on C." While on Y, Ground Control told us to "keep your speed up to cross Runway 4 on Charlie. Company [aircraft] on a four-mile final."  I could not maintain or increase my speed because I still had two turns to make in order to cross Runway 4 (from Y onto C and a slight jog crossing 4). The company on final looked close. 

I asked the First Officer to confirm with Ground Control that we were definitely cleared to cross but he received no response. I was already slowing and, when no response was received, I opted to stop but could not do so in time and went past the hold short line 10 or 15 feet. We then saw a small prop on takeoff roll. The First Officer told Ground we were past the hold short line but, again, got no response from Ground. I got on the radio and forcefully reiterated that we were past the hold short line. (Company was now on short final.) 

Ground said, "Just hold where you are."  The other carrier continued its takeoff roll past us and the company was now on the go [around]. Ground then cleared us to cross Runway 4 and taxi C, M, to Runway 30L. Nothing else was said to us and our takeoff was uneventful.

synopsis: A small aircraft pilot crossed the hold short line for Runway 36R at NEW without clearance. Pilot notes confusion with airport construction as a contributing factor.
narrative:
We filed an IFR departure from NEW in the aircraft were myself and my wife. We picked up the IFR clearance and began our taxi. Prior to taxi I notified the Ground Controller that I had not flown out of this airport in quite a while and was unfamiliar with the ground environment due to the construction and to please keep an eye on us to make sure we were going correctly, particularly since there was so much construction activity with people and equipment in fluid motion, and to verbally assist me along the way. ATIS: winds were 060 at 17 gusting to 25, visibility was 10+, skies were clear. Temperature was 11/dewpoint was -9 and the altimeter was 30.42. The active runway was 36L and visual approaches were being used to that runway. The ATIS recording was very long and included all of the taxiway and runway closures--it was spoken very fast and had to be reviewed 2 or 3 times to get all of the data and was difficult to understand. This needs to be corrected. NEW is currently a dynamic construction zone with infrastructure work ongoing. It was evident by all of the taxi and runway closures, the ground crews, the transition of closed taxiways (i.e. on arrival a taxiway was open that was closed two days later for departure) so, there was constant activity. As a matter of fact as we were taxing out, work crews were waving at us so distractions were aplenty. Our taxi instructions were to exit the FBO cross Runway 9, take Taxiway Echo to Taxiway Hotel. We stopped at the runup pad on Taxiway Hotel and double checked all instruments. I then resumed my taxi to Runway 36L which was in my mind the active runway due to the ATIS announcement. I inadvertently crossed the hold line at the approach end of Runway 36R, a short, mid-field runway. I immediately stopped and was about 1/3 inside the runway threshold. Immediately I assessed the situation, checked for traffic both on the ground and in the air and when I saw none, quickly taxied to the other side of Runway 36R rather than doing a 180 degree maneuver because the latter would have taken more time and would put me in a blocked visual situation for traffic.

At no time prior to the runway incursion, up to the run-up area and then after leaving the run-up area did I hear from Ground Control. Remember my aforementioned statement that notified the Ground Controller that I was unfamiliar and to monitor my progress and notify me if I deviated. When I was clear of 36R on Taxiway Hotel I immediately came up on the Tower frequency 119.9 and acknowledged my mistake and asked for instructions. The Controller cleared me to Runway 36L via Hotel and Bravo. As I neared the approach end of 36L on Bravo, I asked for approval to go full length and was given the okay. I was also asked to take down a number. I queried the Controller whether I should call in the aircraft then or at my destination. He said the destination would be fine. I was then cleared to takeoff and fly runway heading, which I did and then changed to Departure Control 133.15 for radar vectors onto my flight plan. Upon arrival at [my destination] I called the number given to me and spoke with ATC. He indicated that I had a runway incursion, that he had reviewed the tapes and that a report would be filed and I would probably hear from a FSDO. synopsis: Aerostar pilot lands on runway while Citation is still on the active runway.
narrative: Aerostar was arriving to land at WDG and reported 15 miles south of the airport. AWOS was reporting winds as calm but the Tower Controller instructed the Aerostar to report mid-field left downwind for 17. A few minutes later a Citation reported 18 miles out to the west. He was instructed to report 5 mile final for 17. When the Aerostar reported mid-field the Tower Controller did not give landing instructions but instead asked the Citation where he was. He said he was turning 5 mile final now. The Tower Controller cleared him to land. Then the Controller asked the Aerostar if he had the traffic in sight. The response was no and that the Citation was not where he said he was and it was dangerous with the two aircraft heading straight at each other. The Controller's instructions were to continue downwind. He asked the Citation where he was and now the reply was turning 2 mile base to final so the Citation pilot was obviously lying about his previous position. The Controller asked the Aerostar where he was and does he have the traffic. The reply was no and the Aerostar pilot said he would continue on downwind. The Controller advised the Aerostar it was clear to turn base now as the Citation was on 2 mile final. The Aerostar turned base and then final at about 4 miles out. At about 2 miles the Controller again asked if the Aerostar if he had the Citation which was over the numbers in sight and again the reply was no. The Aerostar pilot spotted the Citation on the numbers and informed the Controller. He was cleared to land. The Aerostar put down full flaps and prepared to land reducing power. When the Aerostar was at about 1 mile from the threshold the Controller said to be prepared to go around. When the Aerostar was approximately 25 feet above the runway, the Controller instructed him to go around. The Citation was stopped on the runway at the far end. There was no way for the Aerostar to avoid putting the plane on the ground. The pilot determined there was not enough runway between he and the Citation [to] do a touch and go by powering up and bringing the flaps from full to 20 degrees and safely clear the Citation. He determined there was plenty of space to land and safely stop. The Aerostar pilot informed the Controller that he was unable and putting it on the ground. The landing was made without further incident. The problem was caused by the following actions: 1) The Citation pilot cut the corner and did not go to the 5 mile final point as instructed. The error was compounded when he lied about his actual position to the Controller. The Tower Controller does not have radar so he is relying on aircraft to truthfully and accurately report their positions. If this is not working, then all towers should have radar. 2) The Controller should not have advised the Aerostar to turn base so soon. There was no traffic following and the Aerostar pilot was fine with continuing downwind further. Advising the Aerostar pilot to start his base turn implied there was plenty of separation between the two aircraft which turned out to be not true.  3) Advising a pilot to "Be prepared to go around" is a meaningless instruction and should not be used. The pilot must also be prepared to land. If there is a serious concern the runway might not be clear, the aircraft should be told then to go around at that time, not when they are just about to touchdown. 4) The Citation pilot stopped or nearly stopped on the runway. This behavior is not only in violation of regulations, it is dangerous. It is clear that both the Controller and the pilot of the Aerostar believed there was sufficient time for the Citation to clear the runway.  Stopping on an active runway, especially when it is known that traffic is immediately following, is not only unpredictable and unprofessional, it is dangerous. Ultimately, while no aircraft came within 3,000 yards of each other, this action has caused a great deal of stress on both the pilot and the Controller.

During the confusion caused by the extremely loud noise, I had the aircraft which had landed on Runway 28R as well as the runway edge line continually in sight. I did not see the hold short line until the moment that we had begun to cross it. I immediately brought the aircraft to a stop. We were still approximately 100 FT from the Runway 28R edge line. The aircraft that had landed on Runway 28R before us was exiting the runway, at least two exits away, as we approached the hold short line. After bringing the aircraft to a stop, we were able to re-establish contact with Ground Control by turning off the #2 radio and tuning the Ground frequency with radio #1. We were then cleared to immediately cross Runway 28R and to taxi to parking on the [FBO] ramp. After parking, Maintenance was called to attempt repair of the radio audio panel. It was determined by Maintenance that the panel would require replacement. We remained overnight in San Francisco to accomplish the repair. The unintentional crossing of the hold-short line was a result of the extremely painful distraction in the cockpit. In retrospect, my reaction should have been to immediately stop the aircraft. The noise continued for approximately 15 to 20 seconds. This incident would be categorized as a category "D" runway incursion as there were "no immediate safety consequences" and no aircraft required to abort landing or takeoff, or take any evasive action. Both myself and the First Officer have reviewed, at length, the situation, our reaction to the distraction, and the ways we might avert a situation like this in the future.

synopsis: An AC11 pilot while following a King Air and looking straight on into a bright low-angle sun taxied past the hold short line in MEM.
narrative: I received taxi instructions from MEM Ground and departed the FBO for [Runway] 18C via Taxiway's A & B. When I was getting close to Taxiway S, I received an instruction to contact Tower although I was still taxiing behind a King Air and, either Ground or Tower, I am not sure which, said "follow the King Air." I turned on the B Taxiway and was looking straight on into an incredibly bright low-angle sun. There were several planes cuing up over on C6, C&, & C8, A couple more on the north end of S, and I saw the King air proceed to position. I stopped and immediately felt something was wrong. I was looking for the hold short line in front of me, and thought "un-oh." because I did not see it. Again, the sun was extremely bright. I was nowhere close to Runway 18C so in no way would I call this a "Runway Incursion" and there was no danger created because the King Air was sitting on the threshold, waiting to depart. I had to be at least 100 FT from him, possibly more. I was hesitating calling Tower to ask about the hold short line, because he was rapid-firing off instructions to several planes. I was sure if I switched channels and called Ground, then the Tower would call and I would be off-channel. I did not know if there was a plane behind me at that point, so I was unsure what to do. I was not overly concerned, as no danger was created and there was no chance of a plane having to divert given that the King Air was still holding on the threshold. I was studying the diagram and noticing the "Hot Spot 1" Indication and thinking, "They got that right" and of course, there is no indication on the FAA Runway Diagram where the hold short line would be, or even an ILS hold line. Then the Tower did call, told me to do an immediate 180 and back-taxi on Bravo. I immediately saw the hold-short line. I had passed it the first time by about 15 FT. I complied and in less than 100 FT he told me to 180 again and come back up to the hold short line. After stopping again, with the King Air still holding in position on the runway, I got the instruction to call the Tower after I landed. I did and the Controller at MEM was very informative and courteous and told me he understood the confusion and said "I consider this matter closed." Of course, I have heard sometimes the FAA will review these and conclude differently. In 2,100 hours of flying, this is my first "violation" of a runway marking and I this area was particularly confusing, no doubt why it is a hot spot. I clearly caused no safety issue. I think the markings need to be improved here, and since it is a hot spot, I think they should ward pilots to be particularly aware, and keep them with Ground until they are in the number one holding spot. Having said all of that, I should have noticed the hot spot designation earlier and have been more vigilant. I learned a good lesson here.

synopsis: A PA31 crew lined up for the wrong runway while approaching ORH at night. They realized the error after Tower recleared them to land on the other runway.
narrative: We were cleared for the visual approach to Runway 29 at Worcester Airport, Worcester, MA (ORH) while approaching from the southwest in VMC. The pilot not flying (First Officer), loaded the ILS 29 approach into the navigator, vectors-to-final mode, resulting in navigation to the final approach fix. I was the pilot flying and selected "direct-to" the runway threshold in order to enable a distance to the runway display on the navigator. This procedure disabled the course guidance straight-in to Runway 29. As we approached the airport between a left base to Runway 33 and a left downwind to Runway 29, I saw the green threshold lights of Runway 33, mistaking it for Runway 29. After lining up on Runway 33 the Tower Controller re-cleared us to land, this time for Runway 33, commenting that the wind was aligned with 33. This was my first clue that we were lined up on the wrong runway. I was focused outside the airplane and failed to confirm our heading matched the appropriate runway or utilize electronic guidance. My familiarity with the airport contributed to my complacency, however I had not landed at Worcester at night in many years. The relatively close alignment of the two runways also contributed to my lining up on the first runway I saw. It was a clear example of not taking the extra time to confirm our approach to the proper runway via compass and/or electronic means due to complacency and possibly fatigue. We had been on duty for 9 hours at that point.

synopsis: A solo student pilot practicing in a C172 crossed Runway 18 at GGG without clearance after becoming confused.
narrative: A runway incursion happened when I pulled out across Runway 18.  I believe there were several factors that led to this unintentional mistake. I started the flight knocking off some of the rust as I headed to the practice area. After completing my maneuvers, I headed back to GGG to do some pattern work and various landings. The pattern was busy and became even busier as through a few landings. I was trying to keep a mental note of where each aircraft was, what they were doing, where they were going, what their intentions were and even what they might possibly do. I'm sure that having a full bladder was a distraction as well. I had been doing stop and go's on Runway 18 with left traffic. Upon my last landing I had informed the Tower that I needed to make a change to full stop, taxi backs. This was approved and on landing I was given instructions to exit Runway 18 via left on Bravo and what I thought was left on [Taxiway] November and to hold short of Runway 13. I become really confused as to the Tower's intentions as I repeated back the instructions and "left on November."  There were no corrections as I passed Taxiway Mike (that would have led me back to Runway 18). Holding short of Runway 13 I assumed he might give me Runway 13 via November to clear up some of the traffic on Runway 18. Tower came back to me saying that he may have given me a wrong turn onto November and asked if I could do Runway 18 via Bravo. I said yes and was instructed to make a 180 degree turn on November, right on Bravo to Runway 18. At this point I just got turned around, literally and mentally, without realizing to what extent...yet. I never heard a "hold short Runway 18" and as I repeated back his instructions, he said I was not cleared to takeoff [Runway] 18 but to go there. The misunderstandings continue and confusion grows. At this point I don't remember if the aircraft on Taxiway Mike holding short of 13 was asked, been cleared to or that I comprehend the fact that they are wanting to takeoff. As I stop at the hold short line of Runway 18, I look over my right shoulder to see an aircraft facing me. This is the previously mentioned aircraft wanting to takeoff. At this point the radio is silent, for what I'm sure is not as long as the heat of the moment made this out to be, and I'm now thinking I am on an active for that aircraft's runway (but this runway to speak of is actually Taxiway Mike). At this point of confusion I slowly start to pull across the line thinking that I'm needed to clear the active so he can takeoff. After the front of my airplane crosses the line, I realize that I was correct before I started moving and that I have just crossed the hold short of Runway 18. I now realize that I have to clear the active of 18 via a big 360 to realign on the hold short I just crossed or continue forward and clear the active on the other side. Since I can see and have been watching out in front of me I look both ways and get across. Tower asks what my intentions were and I said I'm just clearing the active and getting out of the way. synopsis: A C172 instructor and student mistook another aircraft's takeoff clearance for their own as they were line up for the runway and did not realize the landing aircraft asked for a takeoff clearance.
narrative: My flight instructor and I were holding short of Runway 32 on Taxiway B at EWB. We had called for takeoff clearance and were told to continue holding short for traffic on short final. The landing traffic has been cleared for "the option" and upon landing the traffic appeared to have asked for take off while still on the runway. The Tower then told the aircraft "cleared for takeoff, keep it rolling". My flight instructor and I mistook the clearance as our own, in the form of an expedited takeoff clearance. (There was an approaching aircraft, so an expedited takeoff made sense). The Controller caught the mistake and told us to stop. We stopped the aircraft and did a quick 180 turn back over the hold short line. We watched the approaching aircraft land from the "safe side" of the hold-short line. Their landing seemed normal, without the use of evasive maneuvers. The landing traffic that had been "cleared for the option" had a very similar call sign, and the Controller's use of abbreviated call signs made our call sign and theirs even more similar sounding. Immediately after the incident, the Controller advised the first landing aircraft not to ask for "the option" but instead be specific in what they wanted clearance for.

synopsis: A C182 unfamiliar with the YIP airport turned early and began back taxiing on Runway 14 instead of the cleared Runway 23R.
narrative: I called for taxi at YIP giving my location on the west ramp and that I would be VFR west bound. I was the only aircraft operating at the airport and the Ground/Tower Controller advised me to taxi to 23L without providing a route of taxi. Unsure of the expected route I requested progressive taxi. The Ground/Tower Controller then requested me to clarify my location and then advised me to taxi to 23R via C, conduct my run up on C and hold short of 23R. I then questioned if I would be getting an intersection departure and what was the available distance. Ground/Tower advised I would be back taxiing on 23R for departure. Following my run up I called holding short and was advised to turn left and back taxi on 23R. Shortly after making the left turn, both I and the Ground/Tower Controller realized I had turn early and was back taxiing on 14. The Controller advised me to continue on 14, turn right on Taxiway G to 23R. The remainder of the taxi, takeoff and flight were uneventful. I believe the contributing factors included fatigue, previous to this flight I had just completed a 3.0 hour IFR flight into YIP. The unfamiliarity with YIP, this was my first flight to the airport, the night near MVFR conditions, and the confusing intersection and markings. Although I was using the G-1000 Safe Taxi feature, I still turned early and missed the turn to back taxi 23R. And although I believe the Controller was trying to help me with a shorter taxi, had I been given the clearance to taxi to 23R via B, G cross 14 it would have been less confusing and avoided a known Hot Spot. Because of the non standardized taxi instructions, I found myself thinking more of what I was expected to do, rather then what I was actually doing.

synopsis: A PA-28R pilot took off without Tower's clearance when they mistook Ground Control's comment of being able to just go as takeoff clearance.
narrative: Departing from AGC on an IFR flight plan in VMC, was given a departure procedure and an intersection departure. I was doing a cargo mission to NYC post storm. I had never done a cargo mission before. The workload loading the plane, accepting an unexpected departure procedure in VFR conditions, being hustled out of the loading area contributed to a large workload. Ground asked if I would be ready to go when I go to the runway and I said yes. I was given an intersection departure which was fine because there was plenty of room. Ground told me that since I didn't have to wait and there was nobody in front of me, I would be able to just go. Well programming GPS etc. I completely misheard and took that as a clearance and departed with out Tower OK. There was no conflict of separation of aircraft and no danger of collision. As soon as I was over the line and powering up the engine, I knew that is not what they meant and knew I was over the line without clearance, but was committed to taking off. Literally couldn't turn around at that point so I departed. Tower instructed me to call them when I landed in NYC which I did. They said no further action was contemplated since there was never a separation issue. They also told me they were training that day as well. In summary - my problem was that I let the situation deteriorate as soon as I let them marshal me out of the load up area. I let external forces rush me through my checklists and normal departure routines and that all added up in the end. Lesson learned is to never let anything get in the way of taking your time and executing your checklists in an orderly manner.

synopsis: Air Carrier Captain attributed a runway incursion on ELP Runway 8 to a confusing taxi clearance.
narrative:
On taxi out from gate in ELP, Ground Control told us to taxi to Runway 8R via Romeo. I took that to mean I was cleared to taxi to the end of Runway 8R, which is over 1,000 FT down from Taxiway R. Normally the clearances in El Paso tell you to hold short of the 8R approach end and this clearance didn't state that. The new ATC phraseology in crossing runways is inconsistent. Under the new phraseology, the clearance I would expect to hear is taxi to Runway 8R via Romeo and hold short of the 8R approach end. The clearance I received led me to think I was cleared to the beginning of Runway 8R without holding short of the approach end. When the Controller notified us what had happened, I told him what I was thinking based on the clearance received. I apologized for the misunderstanding and I wanted to clarify for the future. He said no problem on this end and that they clear you from Romeo so you don't have to taxi Romeo and Mike to 8R and then back taxi on 8R. That whole area is confusing because part of that approach end is also labeled Taxiway Echo.

The new ATC phraseology is arduous. The old phraseology was shorter, more direct, easier to understand, and most of all consistent across the country. Taxiing to a runway mentions taxi to that runway and cleared to cross everything to get to that runway. The new phraseology is inconsistent and adds many more instructions to an already busy and communication overloaded environment. At some airports, the taxi instructions are already very long and now they have to add hold short of all the possible runways and then be cleared across one at a time. It is too much communication. In this situation, the clearance was misunderstood because the Controller did not say hold short of the 8R approach and because that is what I am used to hearing. I assumed it meant I was cleared to the end of 8R. I even told my First Officer when I repeated the clearance that I thought we were cleared to the end of the runway and he thought the same. Confusing, non-standard, communication errors are probably the biggest threat in our environment and clarification is a must. Unfortunately, the clarification adds to more people talking on the radio, more people getting stepped on, and more confusion. Brevity and simplicity in communication is always the best but that is not the way the industry has headed. The other thing that would help is this particular situation is to paint chevrons where the 8R approach is. It would let you know that this area is part of a runway and not a taxiway.

synopsis: Cessna 310 pilot crossed runway hold short line at RVS without clearance.
narrative: I was cleared to taxi to Runway 1L at RVS for departure from the FBO ramp. Before taxi clearance was given there was a problem with the IFR flight plan that should have been filed. I had to contact Flight Service and re-file a flight plan before I started taxiing. During taxi, my copilot and I were discussing why the flight plan was not in the system. I had been to RVS only once before so I had a general idea of where I was going but wasn't quite sure. The hold short line for Runway 1L is set back further than I had expected and the taxiway lead off to the runway was quite wide and I failed to note how close I actually came to the hold short line. My copilot said I was about to cross the line and when I brought the aircraft to a stop, about 3 feet of the aircraft was on the runway side of the hold short line. Just as I came to a stop, Ground Control advised me to hold short of the runway. No other aircraft were on approach to the runway and no further deviations occurred. I failed to have a taxi diagram readily available for reference during taxi; I also had an iPad with an app with geo referenced charts available too, but did not utilize it. Failure to have a sterile cockpit during taxi and discussing the flight plan issues along with the added distraction of passengers asking questions about the upcoming flight contributed to my distraction and failure to keep situational awareness. To keep this from happening again I will initiate sterile cockpit procedures during taxi and only discuss items pertaining to taxiing. I will utilize my iPad and the app to keep situational awareness during surface operations. When carrying passengers I will ask them to hold questions until the airplane has stopped moving on the ground. At unfamiliar airports I will request progressive taxi instructions if available.

synopsis: A BE350 pilot mistook VCT's Runway 36 hold short line for that of Runway 31L crossing over it without clearance.

By the time I brought the airplane to a stop, I was over the line (which was between the nose wheel and the main landing gear). Ground Control said "You are approaching Runway 36. Are you ready for takeoff?" I replied in the affirmative, so they cleared me onto the runway and told me to come up on Tower frequency (same Controller). No mention was made of the incursion and no other traffic was operating at the time. The events from this point forward were routine. I believe that this event occurred for a couple of reasons. First, I had not noticed that I had already crossed the opposite (northeast of the 31L threshold) 31L hold line, so the line that I saw as I approached was not the one I believed it to be and I intended to continue across. Second,the hold line for Runway 36 is quite some distance from the threshold for 36 on an angled taxiway and I thought that I still had some distance yet to taxi. Lesson learned is to always pay attention. The signage and pavement markings were clear and accurate. Just remember that what you think you see and what you really see may be two different things.

synopsis: A BE23 pilot landed on the wrong runway at JRF.

synopsis: CE680 Captain reports a runway incursion taxiing from the FBO ramp via Taxiway B to Runway 19 at FRG. Westbound Taxiway B is followed instead of northbound B.
narrative:
Runway incursion on Runway 19 at FRG. It was a very windy (gusting at times to over 40 knots), with shifting winds and heavy rain. I was the the pilot taxing the plane. Original clearance was to taxi to 19 via Bravo and cross 14. I understood the instructions and looked at it on my iPad. We began taxiing on the [FBO] ramp. Bravo parallels 19 but also does a 90 degree turn and connects to the departure end of 19, which is where the ramp comes out. As we crossed the ramp I was struggling to re engage the gust lock due to the wind and had my partner help push on the rudder to help engage it. We then asked for a wind check, and the winds favored 14 a bit more, so we asked for it and we're provided taxi instructions of Bravo and Alpha to 14. My partner went heads down to change the FMS, but the Honeywell FMS would not accept it because it said the winds were out of limits. I then told ground we would hold our position so I could help with the FMS and figure out what to do. At this time we were located just across the non-movement lines and were almost on bravo. We realized that the FMS's would not take a wind higher than 25 knots no matter if it was a direct headwind or not. The crosswind was not exceeding 25 knots. We then asked for one more wind check and the winds now shifted to 19 (as I said, the winds were very dynamic and gusty). We fixed the FMS and asked for Runway 19 and was told to taxi via Bravo and cross 14. As I began to slowly move the plane I noticed the autopilot fail CAS messages kept coming on and off as well as our AOA vane indicator was fluctuating up and down over and over. I then heard an ELT going off (I had 121.5 set on comm 1 but it was bleeding over to come 2; another side affect of Honeywell). I turned to comm 1 and heard it very loud. I thought it might be coming from us. I may have been reasoning that we might be having an electrical problem; maybe some rain water got on something? I was still taxing slowly; I asked my partner to check the ELT panel to make sure it was on arm, which it was. I looked ahead and saw a location sign indicating I was on Bravo and saw hold short bars for a runway and repeated to my partner "Bravo, cross 14" and he said yes. Things didn't look quite right and I glanced down at my iPad and saw bravo crossed a runway ahead of me but I didn't understand why I would have to take Golf, which was on the other side of the runway, up to 19. I figured I must have missed hearing it because I was preoccupied with the winds, contemplating the best runway to use, with the autopilot issue and the ELT going off. Being on Bravo, as noted by the location sign, I then crossed the hold short lines of a runway. The entire plane was past the line but not on the runway when ground told us quickly to hold our position. I wasn't sure why, but I stopped fast. 

We were then told we entered Runway 19. He then gave us taxi instructions to exit the runway and further instructions to Runway 19. When I came off the [FBO] ramp, even though I was 90 degrees to the parallel Bravo I still saw the Bravo location sign directly in front of me, telling me I was on Bravo. With all the distractions I stayed straight on the short segment of Bravo and entered the runway that was in front of me, which was 19 and not 14. I obviously didn't look at the runway sign. We did however look both ways to make sure it was clear to cross. There was no conflict with any other aircraft. Just to add, the winds shifted again in which we then changed runways again to Runway 14. We taxied there with no further events and all the CAS issues cleared up (we figured it was the gusty winds affecting the AOA, which affected the autopilot). The winds stayed steady favoring 14 with gusts to 30 and we departed 30 minutes later after an ATC delay. 

This was my first ever runway incursion. I am usually very diligent with my taxing and aware of my surroundings.

synopsis: A corporate aircraft expediting taxi for night takeoff incurred HNL Runway 8L at Taxiway E as the First Officer was heads down and the Captain confused by the signage.
narrative: We were under time pressure to depart HNL. We had been in contact with the Tower, Clearance, and Ground Controllers to assure our planned departure time would allow our departure without any undue security delays. Our last discussion in this regard took place with Ground Control when we were told we needed to expedite if we were to be able to depart. We hurried to load our passengers and baggage, start engines, and prepare to taxi. We had worked out a plan with Ground Control to plan an 8L departure from Intersection G. After engine start we contacted Ground for taxi, and were instructed to plan 8L from G, and our route would be C to E, across Runways 4R, and 4L, and then left on B to Intersection G for our 8L departure. We were also told to hold short of 4R at E. We began our taxi, and were told to monitor Tower. We reached E at 4R quickly, and after a short delay, were told by Tower to cross Runways 4R, and 4L, then join B to G, and hold short of 8L. Once taxiing was resumed I was head down in the cockpit, running the taxi/before take-off checklist, when I heard an airliner cleared for take-off on 8L, and virtually concurrent with that instruction was a takeoff clearance cancellation, and the Tower telling us we had missed the turn onto B. The Captain had realized our position mistake, and had stopped the airplane, but we had crossed the hold short lines, at which point he asked if we were on the runway. I looked up, and realized as did the Captain, we had crossed the hold short lines, which now head up, and aware of the situation, came to realize the markings on the runways, taxiways, and even the hold short line for the runway, are very poorly marked, and very poorly lit. This particular area of the airport seems to be a very confusing array of taxiways, runways, and other service roads, lacking quality marking we commonly see at other major airports. After crossing the runway, and continuing our taxi on A, now to hold short of G, we were given a phone number for HCF Control, for a possible pilot deviation. All things stacked on top of each other, night, time pressures of trying to leave the airport expeditiously, lack of familiarity of the given taxi route, poor lighting, and signage, at this particular hot spot, along with only one pilot head up, all were contributing factors to this incident. Certainly wag lights at this hold short position on 8L would have mitigated this incident, or even a much more clearly marked, and lighted taxi pathway would have assisted in avoiding the incident. Lastly the use of ground transponder was a great aid to avoid a far worse outcome to this incident.

synopsis: An air carrier crew cleared to LFT Runway 4R taxied all the way to the Runway crossing Runway 4L but stopping prior to Runway 11 because they thought the taxi clearance included crossing intervening runways.
narrative:
After pushback at Lafayette Airport, we contacted Ground Control for taxi clearance. The clearance consisted of "Taxi to Runway 4R" via Bravo and Juliette. After receiving the clearance, and prior to taxi, I confirmed with the First Officer and verified the taxi clearance with the airport diagram. We started moving straight ahead via Bravo and momentarily stopped on 4L to do our normal safety visual clearance (Left and Right) and then, continued taxi toward Juliette. After reaching Juliette, and turning right, we stopped before crossing Runway 11. When we stopped, we received a call from Ground Control with a possible Pilot deviation, and they also gave us a phone number to contact them. After the call, we received clearance to cross Runway 11 and continue Taxi to 4R. At the end of the runway, on the holding short area, I called the Tower. They informed me that we crossed 4L without clearance.

We never had the intention to cross any active runway. However, with the clearance that we received (and verified with the airport diagram), we understood that we were clear to taxi all the way to 4R, including crossing the Runways (4L and 11). Apparently, my First Officer misunderstood the taxi clearance because, usually the normal taxi clearance instructions are "Taxi Runway 4R via Bravo and hold short Runway 4L." After that, we usually receive further clearance.  

In my opinion, since Juliette Taxiway is at the end of Bravo, and prior to Juliette is Runway 4L, when we received the clearance instructions the way we got them, it became confusing and created an involuntary error. Again, we understood, we were cleared to taxi to Runway 4R, via Bravo and Juliette.

synopsis: CNO Controller described a near conflict event when traffic on final landed on a parallel runway with traffic about to depart, the Controller noting the sun position and window shade condition as problematic.
narrative: I was instructing a Developmental on Local Control. A C172, student pilot on a cross country solo, reported at the Highway 91/Interstate 15 intersection, located southeast of CNO. The Developmental instructed the Skyhawk to make right traffic for Runway 8L. The pilot acknowledged Runway 8L. When the Skyhawk was within 3 miles of the landing runway, the Developmental cleared the Skyhawk to land on Runway 8L. The pilot acknowledged Runway 8L. A Bonanza, requested to depart Runway 8R the Developmental cleared the Bonanza to depart Runway 8R. The Skyhawk was turning right base and appeared to be lining up for Runway 8L. A few seconds later a transmission was heard, asking if the Cessna was landing on Runway 8R. Immediately after that, the C172 transmitted landing Runway 8R. When the Skyhawk was about to cross the landing threshold, I transmitted "Bonanza, cancel take off clearance, hold short of Runway 8R." The Bonanza acknowledged the hold short instructions and never crossed the Runway 8R hold short markings. The Cessna crossed the threshold at about 300 FT AGL and landed on Runway 8R. I instructed the C172 to turn left onto Runway 3 and hold short of Runway 8L. The pilot acknowledged, hold short of Runway 8L. The Skyhawk did not turn on Runway 3. I then told the C172 to turn off the runway and again to hold short of Runway 8L. The pilot turned off Runway 8R at Lima and did not acknowledge the hold short instructions the second time. I had to give detailed taxi instructions to the C172 and to cross Runway 8L at Delta. The pilot acknowledged the runway crossing and crossed Runway 8L. When the C172 had exited Runway 8R, I cleared the Bonanza for takeoff on Runway 8R. The Control Tower is located north of Runway 8L/8R. During the time of the incident, the sun was located low over the horizon, reducing the visibility for the Tower to observe the final legs for both Runway 8L/R. A ridge line, located 4 to 6 miles west of the airport, which runs northwest to southeast, adds to the difficulty of observing aircraft landing on both runways. The aircraft "blend in" with the color of the terrain when their altitudes are below the top of the ridge line, especially when the sun is low over the horizon. Another factor which increases the difficulty of observing the aircraft are the window shades. The Tower window shades, even clean, have numerous scratches, adding to the observation difficulties. During the next 20 minutes, pilots on left downwind (north of the runways) were reporting that they were unable to visually observe the aircraft they were instructed to follow due to the location of the sun. After the incident, the Tower shades were raised and I put sun glasses on to help see the aircraft on final. I recommend the Tower shades be replaced with new ones to improve Tower visibility.

synopsis: PA44 pilot reports clearing the final approach path with a 360 degree turn before announcing a takeoff on CTAF.  An antique aircraft executes a go-around as the reporter enters the runway.
narrative:
I was departing. After the completion of my runup, I completed a 360 degree turn in order to check for traffic prior to departing on Runway XX. I stopped the aircraft at a 45 degree angle to the hold short line, pointing the aircraft to final so that I could have the best view of final approach. I heard an aircraft call base to final for [Runway] XX, and I spotted that aircraft, approximately 3 miles out. I made a radio call that I was "departing Runway XX" and began to taxi into position. While doing so, I saw an antique tailwheel aircraft conduct a go-around above me. I continued with the takeoff, as to not cause issue with others in the pattern, especially with the aircraft on final. I offset my departure leg to the right, as I was faster than the aircraft ahead of me (that conducted the go-around).

I have spent the last 2 days thinking about how I, a seasoned pilot, CFI, and FAA safety team member could have made such an error. The events were 100% my fault, and there were numerous compounding factors that I now realize.
1) The aircraft on short final did not have a radio.
2) I fixated on the aircraft that called base to final, not scanning all of final.
3) I was picking up an aircraft from a paint shop, so I had potential mechanical issues on my mind. 

The main reason I am providing this report, is that I was shocked that I was very deliberate in checking final prior to departure, and yet I still missed the aircraft without a radio. I will now emphasize to my students that we have blind spots. We can not fixate on an object or a space and expect to see all the objects in that space. We must continually scan to pick up any conflicts. The pilot in the antique aircraft did a good job seeing and avoiding. I wish, he had a radio, only so that I could contact him to express my apologies. I was not negligent or taking shortcuts. I am adamant about checking for traffic. We will never stop learning in aviation, and this was a wake up call, and a great lesson for me. Doing things right is very important, because even then, you have room to do it better. I am glad that this experience has educated me further, so that I may continue to educate and promote safety in aviation.

synopsis: An Instructor Pilot reported ABQ ATC seemed overloaded on a Saturday night and while acting as the TRACON. Ground Control and Tower was not aware of the lack of airport lighting during dusk and night conditions.
narrative: I am a flight instructor and had an occurrence at ABQ that I feel should be brought to someone's attention. I was on a multiengine cross country with a commercial student, two hour day and two hour night first leg VFR, second leg IFR. We were being vectored by Albuquerque Approach Control a few minutes before civil twilight. Approach told us to advise them when we had the runway in sight. My student did not see it at that time. He then told us that the runway was at 11 o'clock and to advise when the runway was in sight. My student still did not see the runway. Then Approach told us that he was setting us up for a two mile final for Runway 3 and again to advise when the runway was in sight. I pointed out to my student where it was, not very visible. My student reported to Approach that he had the runway in sight; I don't think that he did. After he said runway in sight, Approach said that he would tell Tower to turn the runway lights up for us and to let them know if they were too bright. And contact Tower. Turning the 2 mile final the lights turned on (I don't think that they were on at all before) and I heard my student say "OH," like he was amazed that the runway was that close. I was not sure if they didn't have the lights on by accident or if they were messing with us. It was getting very dark and I could see the black outline of what looked like an unlighted runway. Leaving Albuquerque an hour and a half later, we were parked at an FBO and called Clearance Delivery to get our IFR clearance before engine start. Clearance was talking to other aircraft as Departure/ Approach. We checked our frequency and it was correct. He told us to hold on so he could find our flight plan while he was talking to other aircraft on Approach/Departure, gave us our clearance and told us to tell him when we were ready to taxi (did not tell us to contact ground). We started our engines and my student told him on clearance frequency, "Aircraft X is ready to taxi." Clearance told us to "Aircraft X, taxi to Runway 8 via Kilo Echo 1 or just Echo 1." My student looked at me confused because he called us twin diamond. My student couldn't find Kilo and asked for progressive taxi. Clearance told us to switch to his frequency on Ground for progressive. We switched to Ground frequency and he gave us progressive. He asked my student if he saw a large 727 parked in front of him. I noticed that the taxiway lights were not turned on or the taxiway signs. We held short of the runway hold short line on E1 and performed a run-up. We advised him that our run-up was complete and he cleared us for takeoff on Runway 8. My student followed the line with our taxiway light, lined up with center of displaced threshold and began advancing the throttles for takeoff. I hit the brakes and pulled his hand off the throttles and showed him that we were not on runway heading. We were lined up for Runway 12, not Runway 8. We turned left and lined up with Runway 8, while lining up on Runway 8 my student verified the heading and took off. It seemed like at night on Saturdays, Clearance Delivery, is Ground, Tower, and Approach/Departure. They also seem to be having runway/taxiway lighting problems. They keep turning the lights on and off. There is also only one hold short line for two runways with headings that are forty degrees off from each other. It seems like an unfamiliar pilot could possibly have a runway incursion at this airport.

synopsis: Tower CIC described a go around event prompted by a departure crossing the runway hold line. Snow covering the taxiway was listed as a causal factor.
narrative:
A Citation jet was taxied out for a Runway 35R at A16 Intersection departure. It was snowing with visibility reduced to 1.5 miles and winds were gusting out the north approaching 25 KTS and the blowing snow was covering most of the east west connectors and obscuring the hold lines. The Citation jet made the turn at A16 and I observed him cross the hold lines with his entire aircraft yet stop well clear of the runway. I hesitated to inform the 2 FLM's on Local, 1 [was] training and 1 instructing, because I had little faith the results would turn out satisfactorily or safely plus there was a Certified Ground Controller/non-CPC working Ground Controller who was also oblivious to the situation. I knew the aircraft was well clear and would be no factor for the arrival but my conscience got to me. I informed the local controllers that the Citation jet appeared to be completely across the hold line at which point the FLM Trainer picked up the binoculars and agreed with my observation. Instead of fixing it, he/she let the FLM Trainee try to fix it with guidance and it went downhill after that. She said lets see if he can side step (meaning the arrival) but the Trainee quickly keyed up to cross the Citation jet with the Learjet inside a mile final. I yelled out no at the same time the FLM Trainer did and the trainee cancelled the crossing but that was too late as the Citation jet hit the gas and began moving and then slid on the taxi up to the runway as the Learjet was very short final and then they sent the Learjet around. It didn't help that both FLM's were sitting and not fully scanning the runway environment. I was on CIC and I was standing and walking around the Tower keeping an eye on the operation. 

Do not have low time FLM's training low time FLM trainees in situations that could mean life and death. The first course of action should have been to send the Learjet around as he was too close to sidestep to Runway 35L. I should have spoken up sooner as the 5-10 seconds I knew about it could have given them the few seconds to make the correct call. Even in snowy conditions, the Local Controller needs to get off their seat and look to make sure their runways are clear and safe. When I was contemplating about informing them, they were both sitting down and not scanning the runway environment. I teach all of my trainees to stand while working for that very reason as it keeps you on your toes, of course having a radio in the Tower helping to keep us awake during slow times would help as well.

synopsis: After diverting to an enroute airport due to the failure of their left generator the flight crew of a C-550 began to cross a runway--believing they had been cleared to do so--but were stopped by Ground/Tower advising they had not been cleared. The pertinent transmission may have been partially blocked.
narrative:
When our left generator appeared to have failed mechanically while enroute, we elected to divert to a nearby airport. We shot the ILS to Runway XX and everything went as planned, good CRM all the way to the ground. 

After landing we cleared the runway and ATC gave us taxi instructions to our selected FBO. As we approached Runway XX at Taxiway Delta we asked if we were cleared to cross. ATC's response was partially blocked but I thought I heard that we were cleared to cross Runway XX at Delta. I read back, "...cleared to cross Runway XX at Delta".  There was no response from ATC. We cleared the runway left and right before proceeding across the runway. As we crossed ATC stated that we were not cleared to cross. At that point we were already across the runway.

We were using NOS charts which were very difficult to use versus the commercially published charts which we are planning on using from now on.

Although there seemed to be good communications going on I believe we must have been blocked by another aircraft. This possibility was increased because ATC was using the Tower frequency for both Ground and Tower operations.
